videos.topic: I have saw vs I have seen — irregular past participle
videos.hook: SAW is what you use alone. SEEN always needs HAVE. Most learners mix this up every single day.

scenes.voice_line: I have <emphasis level="strong">saw</emphasis>. <break time="0.5s"/> No. Never. Not once. Here is the fix that sticks <emphasis level="strong">forever</emphasis>.

scenes.text: ❌ I have saw that movie three times.
scenes.voice_line: You said: I have <emphasis level="strong">saw</emphasis> that movie three times. <break time="0.3s"/> Every single native speaker just felt <emphasis level="strong">physical pain</emphasis>. Let me explain why.

scenes.text: SAW = simple past. Alone. It is complete.
scenes.voice_line: <emphasis level="strong">SAW</emphasis> is the simple past of <emphasis level="strong">SEE</emphasis>. It stands completely alone. I saw the movie. Done. Complete. You do not pair <emphasis level="strong">SAW</emphasis> with <emphasis level="strong">HAVE</emphasis>. Ever. <emphasis level="strong">SAW</emphasis> is the past. It is already finished.

scenes.text: ✅ I have SEEN that movie three times.
scenes.voice_line: <break time="0.5s"/> Say it right: I have <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> that movie three times. <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> is the past participle. It pairs with <emphasis level="strong">HAVE</emphasis>. Have seen. Has seen. Had seen. Always <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> with a helper.

scenes.text: The partner rule: SAW alone. SEEN + HAVE.
scenes.voice_line: Here is the partner rule. <break time="0.3s"/> <emphasis level="strong">SAW</emphasis> is a solo traveller. I saw it last night. <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> is a partner — it needs <emphasis level="strong">HAVE</emphasis> or <emphasis level="strong">HAS</emphasis> or <emphasis level="strong">HAD</emphasis> beside it always. Have you <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> it? She has never <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> snow. I had <emphasis level="strong">SEEN</emphasis> it before.
<break time="0.3s"/> And this is the same pattern for many irregular verbs. Went alone. Have gone. Ate alone. Have eaten. Did alone. Have done. Once you see the pattern, you lock it in forever.

scenes.text: Have you SEEN enough? Or still saying SAW? 🔄
scenes.voice_line: Have you <emphasis level="strong">seen</emphasis> enough? <break time="0.3s"/> Or are you still saying I have <emphasis level="strong">saw</emphasis>?

videos.topic: Countable vs Uncountable nouns — the grammar superpower that fixes a dozen mistakes
videos.hook: One rule. Fixes a dozen grammar mistakes. Most learners have never even heard of it.

scenes.voice_line: <emphasis level="strong">One</emphasis> rule. <break time="0.3s"/> Fixes twelve grammar mistakes. Most learners have <emphasis level="strong">never</emphasis> heard it.

scenes.text: Countable vs Uncountable: every noun is one of these.
scenes.voice_line: Every English noun — <emphasis level="strong">every single one</emphasis> — is either countable or uncountable. <break time="0.3s"/> This is the <emphasis level="strong">foundation</emphasis>. Learn this and articles, quantity words, plurals — all of it clicks into place.

scenes.text: COUNTABLE: can be counted. Has a plural.
scenes.voice_line: <emphasis level="strong">Countable</emphasis> nouns can be counted. <break time="0.2s"/> One apple. Two apples. Three books. One question. Ten mistakes. They have a <emphasis level="strong">plural</emphasis>. You can use <emphasis level="strong">a</emphasis> or <emphasis level="strong">an</emphasis> with them. A book. An apple.

scenes.text: UNCOUNTABLE: cannot count it. No plural.
scenes.voice_line: <emphasis level="strong">Uncountable</emphasis> nouns cannot be counted as individual items. <break time="0.2s"/> Water. Music. Love. Advice. Information. Happiness. You <emphasis level="strong">cannot</emphasis> say one water or two musics. No plural. No a or an. Use <emphasis level="strong">some</emphasis> or <emphasis level="strong">any</emphasis>.

scenes.text: Common villain mistakes: informations, advices, furnitures
scenes.voice_line: Here are the <emphasis level="strong">villain</emphasis> mistakes that come from not knowing this. <break time="0.3s"/> <emphasis level="strong">Informations</emphasis> — no. Information never gets a plural. <emphasis level="strong">Advices</emphasis> — no. Advice is uncountable. <emphasis level="strong">Furnitures</emphasis> — no. Furniture stays singular. These are the top three.

scenes.text: The fix: some information. Some advice. Some furniture.
scenes.voice_line: <break time="0.3s"/> The fix is instant. Some information — not informations. Some advice — not advices. Some furniture — not furnitures. Some or any or a piece of — these are your uncountable helpers. Use them.

scenes.text: Test every new noun: Can I say TWO of it?
scenes.voice_line: Here is your test <break time="0.3s"/> for every new word you learn. Can you say <emphasis level="strong">TWO</emphasis> of it? Two books — yes — countable. Two waters — sounds weird — uncountable. Two advices — never — uncountable. Two of it? Countable. Weird? Uncountable.

visual.test_question: Can you say TWO of it?

scenes.voice_line: Twelve mistakes. <break time="0.3s"/> One rule. Most learners have <emphasis level="strong">never</emphasis> heard it.
